talk: Every time you raise money, you sell a slice of the company, and everyone who already owns a piece ends up with a smaller share. That's dilution. It's fine as long as the pie grows faster than your slice shrinks.

terms.meaning: Your share getting smaller because new shares were issued.
One fundraise: seed, Series A, Series B and so on.
Your share times what the whole company is worth.

questions.prompt: You own 60% of the club. A new investor buys 20% in a new round. What do you own after?
questions.hint: Everyone keeps 80% of what they had.
working: Everyone keeps 100% - 20% = 80% of what they had.
whyNot: 60% x 20% = 12% is the part of your stake that's diluted away, not what's left.
60% - 20% = 40% takes the whole 20% from you. All the old owners share the dilution.
Your share can't stay the same when new shares are issued.

questions.prompt: Before the round the club was worth $10M. The investor put in $2.5M for 20%, so it's now worth $12.5M. What's your 48% worth?
questions.hint: Your new share times the new value.
working: Before the round your 60% was worth $10M x 60% = $6M. Your slice shrank, the pie grew, and your stake is worth the same.
whyNot: $10M x 48% = $4.8M uses the old value. After the round the club is worth $12.5M.
$12.5M x 60% = $7.5M forgets the dilution. You own 48% now.
$12.5M is the whole club, not your 48%.

questions.prompt: The money builds a new stand and a year later the club is worth $20M. What's your 48% worth now?
working: Without the raise you'd own 60% of a $10M club, worth $6M. Dilution paid off because the club grew.
whyNot: $6M is what your stake was worth before the club grew.
$20M x 60% = $12M forgets the dilution. You own 48%.
$20M is the whole club, not your 48%.

penalty.prompt: You own {stake} of the club. A new investor buys {sold} in a new round. What do you own after? (As a percentage.)
penalty.hint: Everyone keeps the same share of what they had.
working: Everyone keeps {1 - sold|pct} of what they had.

traps.why: That takes the whole round out of your stake. All the old owners share the dilution.
That's the slice diluted away, not what you keep.

call.title: How much to raise
call.prompt: Investors value the club at $10M before the money. Raise $2.5M by selling 20% to modernise the stadium, worth 1,000 more fans a match. Or raise $10M by selling 50% for the stadium and a training centre, worth 1,500 more fans a match. Or raise nothing.

options.label: Raise $2.5M for 20%
options.result: Good call. The stadium adds 1,000 x $18 = $18,000 profit a matchday, and you keep most of the club.

options.label: Raise $10M for 50%
options.result: 1,500 x $18 = $27,000 a matchday is only $27,000 - $18,000 = $9,000 more than the smaller raise, for 50% - 20% = 30% more of your club.

options.label: Raise nothing
options.result: No dilution, but no growth either. 1,000 x $18 = $18,000 a matchday left on the table.

takeaway: Dilution is fine when the pie grows faster than your slice shrinks.
